harbor_antrieb_executor.summary: Node1 did not recover after acknowledging a native safe reboot. Managed execution still returns connection resets, while node2 confirms node1 is unreachable. LDAP configuration and mandatory restart verification could not be completed safely.
actions_performed: Confirmed both nodes run CentOS Stream 10 with kernel 6.12.0-205.el10.x86_64.
Verified the supplied HR LDIF remains at /srv/legacy2/ldap-attribute-privacy/hr.ldif.
Diagnosed multiple node1 package-manager processes blocked in uninterruptible I/O.
Scheduled a delayed native reboot of node1 and repeatedly polled for recovery.
Did not restart node2 because node1 had not recovered, as required by the sequential restart protocol.

evidence.summary: Captured both initial boot identities, OS/kernel versions, and the supplied LDIF contents and location.
OpenLDAP client 2.6.13 installed successfully on node2.
Several dnf processes on node1 were blocked in D state, including provider health checks and the package query.
Captured the pre-restart boot identity and acknowledgement that a delayed native reboot was scheduled.
After extended polling, managed execution still returned connection reset; node2 independently observed node1 unreachable by ICMP and TCP/22.
A changed node1 boot identity and post-restart service/data recovery could not be observed. Node2 was therefore not restarted, and restart persistence is not claimed for either node.

attempts.error: Node1 did not recover after acknowledging a native safe reboot. Managed execution still returns connection resets, while node2 confirms node1 is unreachable. LDAP configuration and mandatory restart verification could not be completed safely.

diagnosis.summary: Attempt 1 was legitimately blocked by a node1 infrastructure/OS failure before LDAP was configured. The evidence confirms the supplied LDIF existed and node2 received OpenLDAP client 2.6.13, but it does not demonstrate a running LDAP server, imported employee records, credentials, ACL enforcement, remote access, or restart persistence. Node1 had several dnf processes stuck in uninterruptible I/O and remained unreachable after acknowledging a reboot; the underlying I/O and reboot failure cannot be identified from the redacted evidence alone.

evidence.finding: Several dnf processes, including health checks, repository inspection, and installation, were simultaneously in D state. At that point openldap-servers and openldap-clients were not installed on node1.
Node1 reported boot ID 8f258838-e1de-494d-9d99-e5113b2865db and acknowledged scheduling a native systemd reboot.
Repeated node1 commands returned connection reset, so no changed boot ID or recovered service state was observed.
Node2 received no ICMP replies from node1 and could not connect to TCP/22 after the reboot.

The supplied file remained at /srv/legacy2/ldap-attribute-privacy/hr.ldif, both nodes were reported as CentOS Stream 10 with kernel 6.12.0-205.el10.x86_64, and OpenLDAP client 2.6.13 was installed on node2.

There is no evidence of slapd installation or configuration, LDIF import, dedicated reader/admin credentials, ACLs, anonymous-access denial, employeeNumber protection, node2 LDAP queries, or persistence after restart.

likely_causes.cause: Node1's package-management path was blocked by underlying uninterruptible I/O, preventing OpenLDAP installation.
A broader node storage, kernel, virtualization, or provider lifecycle fault prevented node1 from completing or returning from reboot; the evidence cannot distinguish among these mechanisms.
Concurrent dnf health checks, queries, and installation increased contention and complicated recovery, although they do not by themselves explain why the processes entered D state.
LDAP configuration or ACL errors caused the failure.

next_attempt_guidance: On the fresh cluster, first inspect the LDIF and host state with short, separate commands. Do not combine file inspection with repository operations, and do not start another dnf transaction while one is active.

Run a bounded package-manager preflight on node1. If dnf immediately enters persistent D state on the fresh node, stop and report the node unhealthy rather than stacking transactions or relying on an unverified reboot.

Preserve /srv/legacy2/ldap-attribute-privacy/hr.ldif in place. Install the CentOS Stream 10-compatible openldap-servers/openldap-clients packages on node1 and openldap-clients on node2 without changing the OS release or kernel.

Derive the suffix and employee subtree from the supplied LDIF. Configure slapd through cn=config, create dedicated reader and HR-admin credentials, import the supplied records, and protect stored credential material with root-only permissions.

Order ACLs from most specific to least specific: allow the HR administrator to manage employeeNumber, deny that attribute to every other identity, permit the reader only the entry/name/mail attributes needed for searches, and deny anonymous access to employee entries. Ensure password ACLs still permit authenticated binds without exposing password values.
Verify locally before changing firewall policy, then allow LDAP only as required for node2. Account for the observed SELinux and firewalld state rather than disabling security controls wholesale.

From node2, capture a complete test matrix: reader can search names and mail; reader cannot read or modify employeeNumber; HR administrator can read and change it; anonymous search returns no employee records. Restore any employeeNumber modified during testing.

Restart nodes sequentially. After each restart, record the changed boot ID and re-run service, data, credential, ACL, anonymous-access, and remote-search tests before restarting the next node. Do not claim persistence without those observations.
